chapter.title: Push off and glide

cards.body: Push off a pool wall, then do nothing at all, and you can slide around 4 metres. If the water is a bed, a push off the wall is sliding across it on your front. **The thinner you make yourself, the further the bed carries you.**
cards.simpler: Push off a pool wall, then do nothing at all, and you can slide around 4 metres. Think of the water as a bed. Pushing off the wall is like sliding across that bed on your front. **The thinner you make yourself, the further the bed carries you.**

cards.prompt: Same pool, same push, twice. The first time you look up at the far wall. The second time your face is down, with your head tucked between your arms. Which glide goes further?

options.text: Looking at the far wall, because you can steer
Face down, head between your arms
Both go the same distance, because only the push matters

whyNot.a: That's steering, not gliding. Lifting your head tips your legs down, and sinking legs drag you to a stop.
whyNot.c: That's the push, not the shape. The same push goes much further when your body is long and level.

cards.reteach: Your body rests on the water like a seesaw. When your head goes up, your legs go down, and sinking legs drag like an anchor. With your head down between your arms you stay flat on the bed, so the push lasts longer.

cards.title: The push
cards.body:
Stand in chest-deep water with your back to the wall and one hand on the edge. Bring both feet up flat against the wall behind you, knees bent. Take a big breath, let go of the edge, put your face in and stretch both arms ahead.

Now **push with both feet, straight along the water, not up**. Your shoulders should be just under the surface as you leave the wall.

Then hold the shape: one hand on top of the other, upper arms squeezing your ears, legs together, toes pointed. A pencil slides. A starfish stops.
cards.simpler: Stand in chest-deep water with your back to the wall and one hand on the edge. Put both feet flat on the wall behind you, knees bent. Take a big breath, let go, put your face in and reach both arms forward. Now **push with both feet, straight along the water, not up**, with your shoulders just under the surface. Then hold still: one hand on the other, upper arms squeezing your ears, legs together, toes pointed. A pencil slides. A starfish stops.

cards.title: Priya's two glides
cards.body: Priya, 34, pushes off at her local pool with her chin up and her eyes on the far wall, so she can see where she's going. Her hips drop, her feet touch the floor after about a metre, and she stands up puzzled. On the second try she uses the same push, but with her face down, her head tucked between her arms and her eyes on the floor tiles. She slides 4 metres and comes up convinced someone has moved the far wall closer.
cards.simpler: Priya, 34, pushes off at her local pool with her chin up and her eyes on the far wall, so she can see where she's going. Her hips sink, her feet hit the floor after about a metre, and she stands up confused. Next time she uses the same push, but **with her face down**, head tucked between her arms and eyes on the floor tiles. She slides 4 metres and comes up sure someone moved the far wall closer.

cards.prompt: Tom pushes off hard, then starts kicking and paddling straight away. He stops after 2 metres, out of breath. What should he change on his next push?

options.text: Push even harder, so the splashing has more speed to work with
Push, make himself long and thin, and stay still until the glide fades
Push upwards, so his body rides higher on the water

whyNot.a: That's more effort, not a better shape. The splashing is what slows him, and a harder push won't fix that.
whyNot.c: That's pushing up, not along. An upward push bobs you up and then down, and the glide dies early.

cards.reteach: In a glide, the push is your only engine. After that, your job is to be a thin shape the water can slide past, and every flailing arm or leg works like a brake. Long and still goes further than busy and short.

cards.title: Let it run out
cards.body:
You'd think the push is the hard part. It isn't. **The hard part is doing nothing afterwards.** Every instinct says kick, paddle, look up. Stay a pencil and let the water slow you down on its own, the way a sledge runs out of hill, while you breathe out a slow trickle of bubbles through your nose.

When you've nearly stopped, use the move from chapter 1: knees in, hands press down, head up, feet down. Stand up without reaching for the wall.

Terry Laughlin built his *Total Immersion* method around this idea: a long, balanced body beats a strong, busy one. Every stroke you learn will start from this shape.
cards.simpler: Pushing isn't the hard part. **The hard part is doing nothing afterwards.** Don't kick, paddle or look up. Stay a pencil and let the water slow you, like a sledge running out of hill, while you breathe slow bubbles out of your nose. Nearly stopped? Stand using the chapter 1 move: knees in, hands press down, head up, feet down. No grabbing the wall. Terry Laughlin's *Total Immersion* method says a long, balanced body beats a strong, busy one. Every stroke starts here.

cards.body: Jo pushes off and glides nicely for a metre, then lifts up to check how far the glide has gone. Up goes the head, down go the legs like the far end of a seesaw, and Jo is standing after 2 metres instead of 4. **The tell: if your feet touch the floor before you decided to stand, your head came up first.**
cards.simpler: Jo pushes off and glides well for a metre, then lifts up to see how far they've gone. The head comes up, and the legs drop like the other end of a seesaw. Jo ends up standing after 2 metres instead of 4. **The sign: if your feet touch the floor before you chose to stand, your head came up first.**

cards.prompt: A friend asks what a good glide feels like. Which answer is right?

options.text: A hard push, then kick hard to keep the speed going
One push, then long, thin and still until it fades
A push angled upwards, so you ride high on top of the water

whyNot.a: That's the kick, which comes next chapter. For now, moving legs break your long shape and slow you down.
whyNot.c: That's pushing up, not along. Angling up makes you bob up and down, and the glide dies early.

cards.reteach: Think of the push as the engine and your body as the shape of the car. You can't add more push halfway through a glide, but you can stop adding brakes: arms long, head down, legs together, nothing moving.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Push off the wall with both feet, straight along the water, and make yourself a long, thin pencil: arms stretched, head between them, legs together. Then stay still and let the glide run out before you stand.
cards.simpler: Push off the wall with both feet, straight along the water, not up. Then **make yourself a long, thin pencil**: arms stretched out, head tucked between them, legs together. Now stay still and let the glide slow down on its own before you stand up.

cards.body:
Tonight, in a doorway: stretch both arms overhead, one hand on top of the other, upper arms squeezing your ears, chin slightly tucked. Hold it for 10 seconds. That's your glide shape, practised on dry land.

Tomorrow: why a bigger, splashier kick usually moves you less, not more.
cards.simpler: Tonight, stand in a doorway. Stretch both arms over your head, one hand on top of the other, upper arms squeezing your ears, chin tucked in a little. Hold it for 10 seconds. **That's your glide shape, practised on dry land.** Think of it as a rehearsal before the real thing in the pool. Tomorrow: why a bigger, splashier kick usually moves you less, not more.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now push off the wall into a long, thin shape, glide 3 to 5 metres face down, and stand up without grabbing anything.

repairedFrom.why: It opens with the filler 'Here's an odd thing about...' before the surprising fact. It then mixes two pictures, a bed and a letter slid under a door, so the hook is muddled before the chapter even starts.
repairedFrom.fix: Open card 1 with 'Push off a pool wall, then do nothing at all, and you'll slide 4 metres.' Cut the letter-under-a-door comparison so only the bed picture is left. Separately, move the 'Tomorrow: why a bigger, splashier kick...' line after the dry-land try card, so it becomes the last line of the chapter.
